Periodic elements in finite type Artin–Tits groups
and stability conditions

Edmund Heng Address: E. Heng: School of Mathematics and Statistics, University of Sydney, Australia Email address: edmund.heng@sydney.edu.au , Anthony Licata Address: A. Licata: CNRS-ANU International Research Laboratory FAMSI and Mathematical Sciences Institute, The Australian National University, Australia Email address: anthony.licata@anu.edu.au and Oded Yacobi Address: O. Yacobi: School of Mathematics and Statistics, University of Sydney, Australia Email address: oded.yacobi@sydney.edu.au
Abstract.

Periodic elements in finite type Artin–Tits groups are elements some positive power of which is central. We give a dynamical characterisation of periodic elements via their action on the corresponding 2-Calabi–Yau category and on its space of (fusion equivariant) Bridgeland stability conditions. The main theorem is that an element β\beta is periodic if and only if β\beta has a fixed point in the stability manifold.

1. Introduction

Let (𝖶,S)(\mathsf{W},S) be a finite type Coxeter system, with associated Artin–Tits group 𝖡\mathsf{B}. The group 𝖡\mathsf{B} acts faithfully by autoequivalences on a 2-Calabi-Yau category 𝒯\mathcal{T}. This realises the Artin–Tits group 𝖡\mathsf{B} as a spherical twist group, a categorical analog of a reflection group. This realisation is important in part because it allows dynamics to be introduced into the study of Artin–Tits groups, parallel to other settings in geometric group theory. In particular, the action of 𝖡\mathsf{B} on the space of Bridgeland stability conditions plays a central role in this dynamical study (see Section 4 for more details). The goal of this note is to give a dynamical description of periodic elements of 𝖡\mathsf{B} – those elements β∈𝖡\beta\in\mathsf{B} such that some non-zero power of β\beta is central – using the action of 𝖡\mathsf{B} on the space of stability conditions. The main theorem is as follows.

Theorem 1.1.

A element β∈𝖡\beta\in\mathsf{B} is periodic if and only if β\beta has a fixed point in Stab𝒞⁡(𝒯)/ℂ\Stab_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathcal{T})/\mathbb{C}.

In the above theorem, the space Stab𝒞⁡(𝒯)\Stab_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathcal{T}) is a distinguished connected component of the space of fusion-equivariant stability conditions on 𝒯\mathcal{T}, considered in [16], and Stab𝒞⁡(𝒯)/ℂ\Stab_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathcal{T})/\mathbb{C} is the quotient by the natural ℂ\mathbb{C} action. In simply-laced type ADE, the space Stab𝒞⁡(𝒯)\Stab_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathcal{T}) is the classical space of stability conditions which appears in the works of Thomas [23], Bridgeland [6] and Brav-Thomas [4]. Theorem 1.1 gives an analog for finite type Artin groups of the characterisation of periodic elements in mapping class groups as those mapping classes which admit a fixed point in Teichmüller space.

The proof of Theorem 1.1 relies on two essential inputs. The first is Bessis’s “Springer theory for braid groups” [3] which allows us to reduce the study of arbitrary periodic elements of 𝖡\mathsf{B} to that of dd-th roots of the full twist, where the positive integer dd is regular in the sense of Springer [22]. In particular, Springer theory provides us with the central charge of the sought-after fixed point for such a dd-th root. The second input is the description of Stab𝒞⁡(𝒯)\Stab_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathcal{T}) as the universal cover of the space of central charges, which is identified with the complexified hyperplane complement studied classically in Coxeter theory [23, 6, 16]. This covering property is our main motivation for using 2-Calabi–Yau categories (as opposed to other categories with an action of 𝖡\mathsf{B}) in the dynamical study of 𝖡\mathsf{B}. In fact, our argument for the forward implication of the main theorem does not make fundamental use of the modular description of the universal cover as a stability manifold, whereas the backward implication does (see Remarks 3.3 and 3.7, respectively).

A dynamical classification of arbitrary elements of 𝖡\mathsf{B} also requires understanding the pseudo-Anosov elements, which we expect to exhibit sink-source dynamics on the boundary of Stab𝒞⁡(𝒯)/ℂ\Stab_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathcal{T})/\mathbb{C}, and which should have positive entropy in the sense of [11]. Categorical frameworks for both pseudo-Anosov autoequivalences and for the boundary of Stab𝒞⁡(𝒯)/ℂ\Stab_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathcal{T})/\mathbb{C} have been considered recently (see e.g. [11, 14, 1] and Section 4).

2. Background

2.1. Artin–Tits groups of finite type Coxeter systems

Let Γ\Gamma be finite type Coxeter graph, that is, one whose connected components are all of type A,B=C,D,E,F,G,H,IA,B=C,D,E,F,G,H,I. Denote the set of vertices of Γ\Gamma by Γ0\Gamma_{0}. There is an ms,tm_{s,t}-labeled edge connecting s,t∈Γ0s,t\in\Gamma_{0} whenever ms,t≥3m_{s,t}\geq 3, and there is no edge between vertices s,t∈Γ0s,t\in\Gamma_{0} when ms,t=2m_{s,t}=2.

The Coxeter group 𝖶\mathsf{W} of Γ\Gamma is a finite group with presentation

𝖶=⟨s∈Γ0∣s2=1,(st)ms,t=1⟩.\mathsf{W}=\langle s\in\Gamma_{0}\mid s^{2}=1,\;(st)^{m_{s,t}}=1\rangle.

The Artin–Tits group 𝖡\mathsf{B} is presented as

(2.1) 𝖡=⟨σs for each s∈Γ0∣σsσtσs⋯=σtσsσt⋯⟩,\displaystyle\mathsf{B}=\langle\sigma_{s}\text{ for each }s\in\Gamma_{0}\mid\sigma_{s}\sigma_{t}\sigma_{s}\cdots=\sigma_{t}\sigma_{s}\sigma_{t}\cdots\rangle,

with ms,tm_{s,t} terms on either side of the equation.

The surjective group homomorphism 𝖡→𝖶\mathsf{B}\to\mathsf{W} mapping σs\sigma_{s} to ss admits a set-theoretic section (positive lift) w↦σww\mapsto\sigma_{w}, where if w=st⋯w=st\cdots is a reduced expression then σw≔σsσt⋯\sigma_{w}\coloneqq\sigma_{s}\sigma_{t}\cdots. In particular, let w0∈𝖶w_{0}\in\mathsf{W} denote the longest element and set Δ≔σw0\Delta\coloneqq\sigma_{w_{0}}.

Let ι:Γ→Γ\iota:\Gamma\to\Gamma be the involution induced by w0w_{0}, i.e. αι⁡(s)=−w0⋅αs\alpha_{\iota(s)}=-w_{0}\cdot\alpha_{s}. By Deligne’s Theorem [9, Theorem 4.21], the centre of 𝖡\mathsf{B} is infinite cyclic and generated by Δ2\Delta^{2} if ι\iota is non-trivial, and by Δ\Delta otherwise. We define the full-twist Θ=Δ2\Theta=\Delta^{2}; so Θ\Theta is always central, but whether or not Θ\Theta generates the center of 𝖡\mathsf{B} depends on Γ\Gamma.

The real vector space Vℝ=⨁s∈Γ0ℝ​αsV_{\mathbb{R}}=\bigoplus_{s\in\Gamma_{0}}\mathbb{R}\alpha_{s} has a symmetric bilinear form (⋅,⋅):Vℝ×Vℝ→ℝ(\cdot,\cdot):V_{\mathbb{R}}\times V_{\mathbb{R}}\to\mathbb{R} given by

(αs,αs)=2,(αs,αt)=−2​cos⁡(πms,t)​ for ​s≠t.(\alpha_{s},\alpha_{s})=2,\ \ (\alpha_{s},\alpha_{t})=-2\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{m_{s,t}}\right)\text{ for }s\neq t.

The Tits representation 𝖶→G​L​(Vℝ)\mathsf{W}\to GL(V_{\mathbb{R}}) is defined on generators s∈𝖶s\in\mathsf{W} by

s⋅v=v−(αs,v)​αs.s\cdot v=v-(\alpha_{s},v)\alpha_{s}.

It is a classical theorem of Tits that this representation is faithful. The set of roots for 𝖶\mathsf{W} is

R:={w⋅αs∣w∈𝖶,s∈Γ0}.R:=\{w\cdot\alpha_{s}\mid w\in\mathsf{W},s\in\Gamma_{0}\}.

We let Vℂ′:=Homℝ⁡(Vℝ,ℂ)V_{\mathbb{C}}^{\prime}:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{R}}(V_{\mathbb{R}},\mathbb{C}). The 𝖶\mathsf{W}-action on Vℂ′V_{\mathbb{C}}^{\prime} is contragradient to that on VℝV_{\mathbb{R}}: for Z∈Vℂ′,v∈VℝZ\in V_{\mathbb{C}}^{\prime},v\in V_{\mathbb{R}}, and w∈𝖶w\in\mathsf{W},

(w⋅Z)​(v)=Z⁡(w−1⋅v).(w\cdot Z)(v)=Z(w^{-1}\cdot v).

(Here we use ZZ to denote vectors in Vℂ′V_{\mathbb{C}}^{\prime} since in the sequel regular vectors in Vℂ′V_{\mathbb{C}}^{\prime} will be central charges for stability conditions.)

2.2. Springer theory for braid groups

We first recall some notions from Springer theory for Coxeter groups [22]. A vector Z∈Vℂ′Z\in V_{\mathbb{C}}^{\prime} is regular if w⋅Z=Zw\cdot Z=Z implies that w=ew=e. An element w∈𝖶w\in\mathsf{W} is dd-regular if it admits a regular eigenvector Z∈Vℂ′Z\in V_{\mathbb{C}}^{\prime} with eigenvalue ζd\zeta_{d}, where ζd\zeta_{d} is a primitive dd-th root of unity. Finally, an integer d∈ℤ>0d\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0} is regular if there exist a dd-regular element in 𝖶\mathsf{W}. The classification of regular integers for finite type Coxeter groups is well-known.

In his seminal work, Springer studied centralisers of regular elements. In particular, he shows that if ww is dd-regular, then its centraliser 𝖶0=C𝖶​(w)\mathsf{W}_{0}=C_{\mathsf{W}}(w) is a complex reflection group acting on the eigenspace ker⁡(w−ζd)\ker(w-\zeta_{d}).

For a root α∈R\alpha\in R, define the hyperplane in Vℂ′V_{\mathbb{C}}^{\prime}

Hα={Z∈Vℂ′∣Z⁡(α)=0}.H_{\alpha}=\{Z\in V_{\mathbb{C}}^{\prime}\mid Z(\alpha)=0\}.

Note that w⁡(Hα)=Hw⋅αw(H_{\alpha})=H_{w\cdot\alpha}. The (complexified) hyperplane complement

ℋ≔Vℂ′∖⋃α∈RHα,\mathcal{H}\coloneqq V_{\mathbb{C}}^{\prime}\setminus\bigcup_{\alpha\in R}H_{\alpha},

is precisely the locus of regular vectors in Vℂ′V_{\mathbb{C}}^{\prime}. The Coxeter group 𝖶\mathsf{W} acts freely on ℋ\mathcal{H}, and choosing any Z∈ℋZ\in\mathcal{H} as a basepoint, there is a group isomorphism 𝖡≅π1​(ℋ/𝖶,Z¯)\mathsf{B}\cong\pi_{1}(\mathcal{H}/\mathsf{W},\overline{Z}), where Z¯\overline{Z} denotes the image of ZZ in ℋ/𝖶\mathcal{H}/\mathsf{W} [25]. The following loop ϑ∈π1​(ℋ/𝖶,Z¯)\vartheta\in\pi_{1}(\mathcal{H}/\mathsf{W},\overline{Z}) plays an important role in what follows:

(2.2) ϑ:[0,1]→ℋ/𝖶,t↦e2​π​i​t​Z¯.\displaystyle\vartheta:[0,1]\to\mathcal{H}/\mathsf{W},\;t\mapsto e^{2\pi it}\overline{Z}.

It follows essentially from [7, Theorem 2.24] that one can choose the isomorphism above so that ϑ\vartheta corresponds to the full twist Θ\Theta; we give an independent proof of this fact later in Lemma 2.10.

Definition 2.3.

A braid β∈𝖡\beta\in\mathsf{B} is periodic if a non-trivial power of it lies in the centre of 𝖡\mathsf{B}. Equivalently, β\beta is periodic if βp=Δq\beta^{p}=\Delta^{q} for some p,q∈ℤ,p≠0p,q\in\mathbb{Z},p\neq 0.

We will now recall Bessis’ remarkable “Springer theory for braid groups”, which is crucial in what follows. One important aspect of this theory is that certain periodic elements – those that appear as positive integral roots of the full-twist – play the role of regular elements for 𝖡\mathsf{B}. More precisely,

Theorem 2.4 ([3], Theorem 12.4).

Let dd be a positive integer, and let ζd=e2​π​id\zeta_{d}=e^{\frac{2\pi i}{d}}.

  1. (1)

    There exists a dd-th root of Θ\Theta if and only if dd is regular for 𝖶\mathsf{W}.

  2. (2)

    Let dd be regular for 𝖶\mathsf{W}. Then there is a single conjugacy class of dd-th roots of Θ\Theta in 𝖡\mathsf{B}.

  3. (3)

    Let β\beta be a dd-th root of Θ\Theta. Let ww be the image of β\beta in 𝖶\mathsf{W}. Then, up to conjugation, ww is dd-regular with eigenvalue ζd\zeta_{d}, and the centraliser C𝖡​(β)C_{\mathsf{B}}(\beta) is isomorphic to the Artin–Tits group corresponding to the Coxeter group 𝖶0=C𝖶​(w)\mathsf{W}_{0}=C_{\mathsf{W}}(w).

2.3. 2-Calabi–Yau categories of finite type Coxeter systems

In this section we recall basic facts about the 2-Calabi–Yau categories associated to finite type Coxeter systems.

2.3.1. Simply-laced type

To begin, we first recall the definition of the 2-Calabi-Yau category when Γ\Gamma is simply-laced and irreducible (that is, of type An,Dn,E6,E7,E8A_{n},D_{n},E_{6},E_{7},E_{8}). There are several approaches to defining this category, see e.g. [2] for an algebraic definition. We recall here the geometric approach to defining 𝒯\mathcal{T}, following [6].

The McKay correspondence associates to any simply-laced finite type diagram Γ\Gamma a finite subgroup GG of S​U​(2)SU(2), and a Kleinian singularity ℂ2/G\mathbb{C}^{2}/G; let

π:YΓ⟶ℂ2/G\pi:Y_{\Gamma}\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}^{2}/G

denote the minimal resolution, and Db​(YΓ)D^{b}(Y_{\Gamma}) the bounded derived category of coherent sheaves on YΓY_{\Gamma}. The 2-Calabi–Yau category 𝒯\mathcal{T} is by definition the full triangulated subcategory of Db​(YΓ)D^{b}(Y_{\Gamma}) containing sheaves EE such that:

  1. (1)

    EE is supported on π−1​(0)\pi^{-1}(0), and

  2. (2)

    R​π∗​E=0R\pi_{*}E=0.

As usual, we let [1]:𝒯→𝒯[1]:\mathcal{T}\to\mathcal{T} denote the homological shift functor.

The graph Γ\Gamma arises as the dual graph of the exceptional divisor of π\pi. The vertices of Γ\Gamma correspond to the irreducible components of the exceptional divisor (which are copies of ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}); the edges of Γ\Gamma correspond to intersection points of the components. For s∈Γs\in\Gamma, let Ps∈Db​(YΓ)P_{s}\in D^{b}(Y_{\Gamma}) be the sheaf is∗​𝒪​(−1){i_{s}}_{*}\mathcal{O}(-1) where is:ℙ1→YΓi_{s}:\mathbb{P}^{1}\rightarrow Y_{\Gamma} is the inclusion of the component of the exceptional divisor indexed by ss. The objects PsP_{s} form a Γ\Gamma-configuration of spherical objects, and 𝒯\mathcal{T} is generated by them as a triangulated category.

The category 𝒯\mathcal{T} is 2-Calabi–Yau, meaning that there are isomorphisms

Hom∙⁡(X,Y)≅Hom∙⁡(Y,X⁡[2])∗\operatorname{Hom}^{\bullet}(X,Y)\cong\operatorname{Hom}^{\bullet}(Y,X[2])^{*}

natural in X,YX,Y, (here (−)∗(-)^{*} denotes the linear dual). In addition, 𝒯\mathcal{T} has a standard tt-structure whose heart is the extension closure of the PsP_{s}, and the spherical objects PsP_{s} are the simple objects of this heart. We denote this heart by ♡std\heartsuit_{\std} in what follows.

The Artin–Tits group 𝖡\mathsf{B} acts on 𝒯\mathcal{T} (on the left) by autoequivalences, with the generator σs\sigma_{s} acting by Σσs\Sigma_{\sigma_{s}}, the Seidel-Thomas spherical twist in the spherical object PsP_{s} [21]. In particular, these autoequivalences satisfy the braid relations (2.1) up to isomorphism. Hence, for any β∈𝖡\beta\in\mathsf{B} we have an associated autoequivalence Σβ\Sigma_{\beta}, which is well-defined up to isomorphism.

As a result, 𝖡\mathsf{B} acts linearly on the real Grothendieck group K0​(𝒯)⊗ℤℝK_{0}(\mathcal{T})\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{R}, with the generator σs\sigma_{s} acting by

[X]↦[X]−χ​Hom∙⁡(Ps,X)​[Ps].[X]\mapsto[X]-\chi\operatorname{Hom}^{\bullet}(P_{s},X)[P_{s}].

Here χ\chi denotes the Euler characteristic, so that if U∙=⊕nUnU^{\bullet}=\oplus_{n}U_{n} is a ℤ\mathbb{Z}-graded vector space, then χ​U∙=∑n(−1)n​dimUn\chi U^{\bullet}=\sum_{n}(-1)^{n}\dim U_{n}. In fact

χ​Hom∙⁡(Ps,Ps)=2,χ​Hom∙⁡(Ps,Pt)=(αs,αt)=−2​cos⁡(πms,t)​ for ​s≠t.\chi\operatorname{Hom}^{\bullet}(P_{s},P_{s})=2,\ \ \chi\operatorname{Hom}^{\bullet}(P_{s},P_{t})=(\alpha_{s},\alpha_{t})=-2\cos(\frac{\pi}{m_{s,t}})\text{ for }s\neq t.

From this, one sees that

  • •

    the action of 𝖡\mathsf{B} on 𝒯\mathcal{T} induces an action of 𝖶\mathsf{W} on K0​(𝒯)⊗ℤℝK_{0}(\mathcal{T})\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{R}, and

  • •

    the resulting representation of 𝖶\mathsf{W} is isomorphic to the Tits representation VℝV_{\mathbb{R}}.

In particular, there is an isomorphism of representations of 𝖶\mathsf{W}

Vℂ′≅Homℤ⁡(K0​(𝒯),ℂ),V^{\prime}_{\mathbb{C}}\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}}(K_{0}(\mathcal{T}),\mathbb{C}),

and elements of Vℂ′V^{\prime}_{\mathbb{C}} may be thought of as homomorphisms from the Grothendieck group of 𝒯\mathcal{T} to ℂ\mathbb{C}.

When Γ\Gamma is simply-laced but not irreducible, so that each connected component of Γ\Gamma is type ADE, we take 𝒯\mathcal{T} to be the product of the categories associated to each connected component.

2.3.2. Non-simply-laced type

In other finite types the construction of the 2-Calabi–Yau category 𝒯\mathcal{T} and the Artin–Tits group action on it is very similar to the one described above; in fact, when Γ\Gamma is not of type ADE, the category 𝒯\mathcal{T} associated to Γ\Gamma is an ADE category as above, equipped with the action of a fusion category associated to the non-simply-laced Coxeter system.

More precisely, in [16], we associate to each Γ\Gamma two pieces of data:

  • •

    a fusion category 𝒞\mathcal{C}, and

  • •

    a simply-laced diagram Γ~\widetilde{\Gamma}, known as the “unfolding” of Γ\Gamma.

Since the precise construction is not used directly in any of the proofs below, we do not give the general definition of 𝒞\mathcal{C} or the unfolding here, but summarise only the essential points. Interested readers can consult [16] for details. We stress that if Γ\Gamma is simply-laced, the fusion category 𝒞\mathcal{C} is just the category 𝗏𝖾𝖼{\mathsf{vec}} of finite dimensional ℂ\mathbb{C}-vector spaces, and the unfolding of Γ\Gamma is Γ\Gamma itself.

The fusion category 𝒞\mathcal{C} and the unfolded diagram Γ~\widetilde{\Gamma} are compatible in that there is a right action of 𝒞\mathcal{C} on the triangulated category 𝒯Γ~\mathcal{T}_{\widetilde{\Gamma}} associated to Γ~\widetilde{\Gamma}. We define the triangulated category associated to Γ\Gamma to be the triangulated module category 𝒯=(𝒯Γ~,𝒞Γ)\mathcal{T}=(\mathcal{T}_{\widetilde{\Gamma}},\mathcal{C}_{\Gamma}); that is, the relevant triangulated category in non-simply-laced type is a simply-laced type category, together with the action of a fusion category on it. (This is not precisely the definition given in [16], but it is equivalent by [16, Proposition 8.4].)

The fusion category 𝒞\mathcal{C} is given by the Fibonacci fusion category 𝖥𝗂𝖻{\mathsf{Fib}}. This is the unique fusion category that has two (non-isomorphic) simple objects 𝟙\mathbbm{1} and Φ\Phi with fusion rules given by Φ⊗Φ≅𝟙⊕Φ\Phi\otimes\Phi\cong\mathbbm{1}\oplus\Phi and 𝟙\mathbbm{1} the monoidal unit [20]. The action of Φ∈𝒞\Phi\in\mathcal{C} on 𝒯\mathcal{T} sends

P1↦P3,\displaystyle P_{1}\mapsto P_{3},\quad P3↦P1⊕P3;\displaystyle P_{3}\mapsto P_{1}\oplus P_{3};
P4↦P2,\displaystyle P_{4}\mapsto P_{2},\quad P2↦P2⊕P4.\displaystyle P_{2}\mapsto P_{2}\oplus P_{4}.

∎

The Grothendieck group K0​(𝒞)K_{0}(\mathcal{C}) is a fusion ring, and the Frobenius-Perron map [13, Definition 3.3.3]

FPdim:K0​(𝒞)⟶ℝ\FPdim:K_{0}(\mathcal{C})\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}

makes ℝ\mathbb{R} and ℂ\mathbb{C} into K0​(𝒞)K_{0}(\mathcal{C})-modules; when 𝒞=𝗏𝖾𝖼\mathcal{C}={\mathsf{vec}}, K0​(𝒞)≅ℤK_{0}(\mathcal{C})\cong\mathbb{Z} and FPdim\FPdim is just the usual dimension map. Thus, in all types, there are isomorphisms of 𝖶\mathsf{W}-modules

Vℝ≅K0​(𝒯)⊗K0​(𝒞)ℝ,Vℂ′≅HomK0​(𝒞)⁡(K0​(𝒯),ℂ).V_{\mathbb{R}}\cong K_{0}(\mathcal{T})\otimes_{K_{0}(\mathcal{C})}\mathbb{R},\ \ \ V^{\prime}_{\mathbb{C}}\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{K_{0}(\mathcal{C})}(K_{0}(\mathcal{T}),\mathbb{C}).

In this way, elements of Vℂ′V^{\prime}_{\mathbb{C}} may be thought of as fusion-ring equivariant homomorphisms from the Grothendieck group of 𝒯\mathcal{T} to ℂ\mathbb{C}.

For later use, we prove that the full-twist acts by a shift on the 2-CY category 𝒯\mathcal{T}:

Lemma 2.6.

The full-twist autoequivalence Θ\Theta acts on 𝒯\mathcal{T} as the Serre functor [2].

Proof.

First suppose that Γ\Gamma is simply-laced. In [15], the authors study a triangulated category 𝒦b​(A−pmod)\mathcal{K}^{b}(A-\mathrm{pmod}), which categorifies the zero weight space in the adjoint representation of the corresponding quantum group. If nn is the height of the highest root, they show that Θ\Theta acts on 𝒦b​(A−pmod)\mathcal{K}^{b}(A-\mathrm{pmod}) by [2​n]​⟨2​n−2⟩[2n]\langle 2n-2\rangle, where the brackets ⟨∙⟩\langle\bullet\rangle denote internal grading shift and [∙][\bullet] denotes homological shift (see [15, Theorems 6.4 & 7.7 and Lemma 7.4]). The 2-Calabi-Yau category 𝒯\mathcal{T} is not exactly the category 𝒦b​(A−pmod)\mathcal{K}^{b}(A-\mathrm{pmod}), but rather is a quotient of it, essentially given by declaring isomorphic the objects X⁡[1]X[1] and X​⟨−1⟩X\langle-1\rangle (see [2, Section 2.3.3] for the precise construction). In particular, it follows immediately that in simply-laced type the full twist acts on 𝒯\mathcal{T} as shift by two.

Now let Γ\Gamma be any finite–type non-simply-laced (i.e. non ADE) Coxeter diagram and Γ~\widetilde{\Gamma} be its unfolding. By [16, Proposition 8.9, Corollary 8.10], the action of 𝖡\mathsf{B} on 𝒯\mathcal{T} factors through the action of 𝖡Γ~\mathsf{B}_{\widetilde{\Gamma}} via an injective group homomorphism 𝖡→𝖡Γ~\mathsf{B}\to\mathsf{B}_{\widetilde{\Gamma}} which sends the positive lift of any Coxeter element of 𝖡\mathsf{B} to the positive lift of a Coxeter element of 𝖡Γ~\mathsf{B}_{\widetilde{\Gamma}} (see [8] and [16, §8.1]). Since positive lifts of Coxeter elements are hh-th roots of the full twist, where hh is the Coxeter number, it therefore suffices to show that 𝖶\mathsf{W} and 𝖶Γ~\mathsf{W}_{\widetilde{\Gamma}} have the same Coxeter number. This can be done via a case-by-case analysis, which is listed in [17, Fig. 2] (another proof of this agreement of Coxeter numbers can be found in [12, Theorem 6.9]). ∎

2.4. Fusion-equivariant stability conditions on 𝒯\mathcal{T}

In this section we collect some essential properties of the action of 𝖡\mathsf{B} on the triangulated category 𝒯\mathcal{T} and on its associated stability manifold. In simply-laced type, the results herein are due to Thomas in type A [23] and Bridgeland in types ADE [6]. For more general Coxter systems they appear in work of the first two authors [16].

Recall that a (Bridgeland) stability condition τ≔(𝒫,Z)\tau\coloneqq(\mathcal{P},Z) on 𝒯\mathcal{T} consists of a slicing 𝒫\mathcal{P} and a central charge ZZ. The slicing 𝒫=(𝒫⁡(φ))φ∈ℝ\mathcal{P}=(\mathcal{P}(\varphi))_{\varphi\in\mathbb{R}} is a one-parameter family of additive subcategories 𝒫⁡(φ)⊂𝒯\mathcal{P}(\varphi)\subset\mathcal{T}, and the objects in 𝒫⁡(φ)\mathcal{P}(\varphi) are referred to as semistable objects of phase φ\varphi. The central charge Z∈Homℤ⁡(K0​(𝒯),ℂ)Z\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}}(K_{0}(\mathcal{T}),\mathbb{C}) is a group homomorphism. This datum satisfies several requirements, the most important of which is a compatibility between the slicing and central charge. We refer the reader to [5] for the precise definition, and mention only the facts we will need here.

The slicing 𝒫\mathcal{P} in a stability condition is a refinement of the notion of a t-structure on 𝒯\mathcal{T}. More precisely, the category 𝒫(0,1]\mathcal{P}(0,1], defined as the extension-closure of the semistable objects of phase φ\varphi for 0<φ≤10<\varphi\leq 1, is always the heart of a tt-structure.

Let Stab⁡(𝒯)\Stab(\mathcal{T}) denote the moduli of stability conditions associated to 𝒯\mathcal{T}. By Bridgeland’s Theorem [5], this is naturally a complex manifold where the local charts are provided by the map taking a stability condition to its central charge. It can be difficult to say much about the stability manifold for arbitrary triangulated categories. However, in the specific case of interest here, Stab⁡(𝒯)\Stab(\mathcal{T}) is fairly well understood. In particular, it is known to be connected [2]. Moreover, it contains a closed submanifold Stab𝒞⁡(𝒯)\Stab_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathcal{T}), which is a distinguished connected component of the space of 𝒞\mathcal{C}-equivariant stability conditions ([10]). Here a 𝒞\mathcal{C}-equivariant stability condition (𝒫,Z)(\mathcal{P},Z) is a stability condition such that

  • •

    each semistable subcategory 𝒫⁡(φ)\mathcal{P}(\varphi) is preseved by the action of the fusion category 𝒞\mathcal{C}, and

  • •

    the central charge ZZ is K0​(𝒞)K_{0}(\mathcal{C}) equivariant, i.e. Z∈HomK0​(𝒞)⁡(K0​(𝒯),ℂ).Z\in\operatorname{Hom}_{K_{0}(\mathcal{C})}(K_{0}(\mathcal{T}),\mathbb{C}).

We note again that if Γ\Gamma is ADE, so that 𝒞=𝗏𝖾𝖼\mathcal{C}={\mathsf{vec}}, then Stab𝒞⁡(𝒯)=Stab⁡(𝒯)\Stab_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathcal{T})=\Stab(\mathcal{T}) is the entire stability manifold, so, at least in simply-laced type, one can ignore any of the additional structure coming from the action of the fusion category.

An autoequivalence Σ\Sigma of 𝒯\mathcal{T} induces a homeomorphism of Stab⁡(𝒯)\Stab(\mathcal{T}), denoted gΣg_{\Sigma}, and defined as follows: for τ=(𝒫,Z)\tau=(\mathcal{P},Z) set gΣ​(τ)=(𝒫′,Z′)g_{\Sigma}(\tau)=(\mathcal{P}^{\prime},Z^{\prime}), where 𝒫′​(φ)≔Σ⁡(𝒫⁡(φ))\mathcal{P}^{\prime}(\varphi)\coloneqq\Sigma(\mathcal{P}(\varphi)) and Z′​([X])≔Z⁡([Σ−1​(X)]CLOSEZ^{\prime}([X])\coloneqq Z([\Sigma^{-1}(X)]. If Σ\Sigma is an autoequivalence of 𝒯\mathcal{T} as a 𝒞\mathcal{C}-module (i.e. Σ\Sigma commutes with the action of the fusion category), then the submanifold Stab𝒞⁡(𝒯)\Stab_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathcal{T}) is preserved by gΣg_{\Sigma}. When the autoequivalence Σ=Σβ\Sigma=\Sigma_{\beta} comes from an element β∈𝖡\beta\in\mathsf{B}, we write gβ≔gΣβg_{\beta}\coloneqq g_{\Sigma_{\beta}} or simply β⋅τ\beta\cdot\tau for the stability condition gβ​(τ)g_{\beta}(\tau).

We summarise the results about stability conditions on 𝒯\mathcal{T} that we need in the following:

Theorem 2.7 ([16, 4, 6]).

We have the following:

  1. (1)

    Stab𝒞⁡(𝒯)\Stab_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathcal{T}) is the universal cover of ℋ/𝖶\mathcal{H}/\mathsf{W}. The covering map π\pi is given by sending a 𝒞\mathcal{C}-equivariant stability condition τ=(𝒫,Z)\tau=(\mathcal{P},Z) to Z¯\overline{Z}.

  2. (2)

    The group 𝖡\mathsf{B} acts faithfully on 𝒯\mathcal{T}, with the Artin generators acting by fusion-spherical twists. The induced action of 𝖡\mathsf{B} on Stab𝒞⁡(𝒯)\Stab_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathcal{T}) is also faithful, and β↦gβ\beta\mapsto g_{\beta} identifies 𝖡\mathsf{B} with the group of deck transformations Deck⁡(π)\Deck(\pi).

  3. (3)

    The subset of 𝒞\mathcal{C}-equivariant stability conditions (𝒫,Z)(\mathcal{P},Z) such that 𝒫(0,1]=♡std\mathcal{P}(0,1]=\heartsuit_{\std} forms a fundamental domain for the 𝖡\mathsf{B}-action on Stab𝒞⁡(𝒯)\Stab_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathcal{T}).

In particular, the fundamental domain of the 𝖶\mathsf{W}-action on ℋ\mathcal{H} can be given by the subset of central charges whose image Z⁡(αs)Z(\alpha_{s}) for all simple roots αs\alpha_{s} lies in ℍ∪ℝ<0\mathbb{H}\cup\mathbb{R}_{<0}, the strict upper half plane union the negative real line.

The deck-transformation action of π1​(ℋ/𝖶,Z¯)\pi_{1}(\mathcal{H}/\mathsf{W},\overline{Z}) on its universal cover depends on the choice of lift of the base point Z¯\overline{Z}. In what follows we fix this lift to be the unique stability condition (𝒫,Z)∈π−1​(Z¯)(\mathcal{P},Z)\in\pi^{-1}(\overline{Z}) whose heart 𝒫(0,1]\mathcal{P}(0,1] is ♡std\heartsuit_{\std}. For λ∈π1​(ℋ/𝖶,Z¯)\lambda\in\pi_{1}(\mathcal{H}/\mathsf{W},\overline{Z}), we let fλf_{\lambda} denote the corresponding deck transformation. (Sometimes, we’ll simply write λ⋅τ\lambda\cdot\tau for the action of λ\lambda on a stability condition.) Thus we have the following isomorphisms:

(2.8) 𝖡\displaystyle\mathsf{B} →≅Deck⁡(π)\displaystyle\xrightarrow{\cong}\Deck(\pi) ←≅π1​(ℋ/𝖶,Z¯)\displaystyle\xleftarrow{\cong}\pi_{1}(\mathcal{H}/\mathsf{W},\overline{Z})
(2.9) β\displaystyle\beta ↦gβ,fλ\displaystyle\mapsto g_{\beta},\ \ f_{\lambda} ↦λ,\displaystyle\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\mapsto$}}\lambda,

the composition of which gives, for any choice of ZZ, an explicit isomorphism 𝖡≅π1​(ℋ/𝖶,Z¯)\mathsf{B}\cong\pi_{1}(\mathcal{H}/\mathsf{W},\overline{Z}). For the following lemma recall that Θ∈𝖡\Theta\in\mathsf{B} is the full-twist and ϑ∈π1​(ℋ/𝖶,Z¯)\vartheta\in\pi_{1}(\mathcal{H}/\mathsf{W},\overline{Z}) is defined in (2.2).

Lemma 2.10.

Under the isomorphism (2.8) we have that Θ↦ϑ\Theta\mapsto\vartheta.

Proof.

Since 𝖡\mathsf{B} acts faithfully on 𝒯\mathcal{T}, it suffices to show that fϑ=gΘf_{\vartheta}=g_{\Theta}. To prove this equality, note ϑ\vartheta lifts to the path ϑ~\widetilde{\vartheta} in Stab⁡(𝒯)\Stab(\mathcal{T}) given by t↦(2​π​i​t)⋅τ0t\mapsto(2\pi it)\cdot\tau_{0}. Since ϑ~​(1)=g[2]​(τ0)\widetilde{\vartheta}(1)=g_{[2]}(\tau_{0}), we have that fϑ=g[2]f_{\vartheta}=g_{[2]}. On the other hand, by Lemma 2.6 the full-twist autoequivalence Θ\Theta acts on 𝒯\mathcal{T} as shift by two. ∎

In order to check whether or not a braid β∈𝖡\beta\in\mathsf{B} acts by the identity functor on 𝒯\mathcal{T}, it is sufficient to check that Σβ​(Ps)≅Ps\Sigma_{\beta}(P_{s})\cong P_{s} for each of the generating spherical objects PsP_{s}. (Using the faithfulness of the action of 𝖡\mathsf{B} on 𝒯\mathcal{T}, this fact gives an algorithm for solving the word problem in 𝖡\mathsf{B}: acting on each of the PsP_{s} in turn and check whether or not the result is isomorphic to PsP_{s}.) Like the identity functor, other shifts [a][a] can be detected by checking the action of β\beta on generating objects. We recall this fact for later use here.

Lemma 2.11 ([16, Proposition 7.26]).

Let β∈𝖡\beta\in\mathsf{B}. If there exists a∈ℤa\in\mathbb{Z} such that for every s∈Γ0s\in\Gamma_{0}, Σβ​(Ps)≅Ps​[a]\Sigma_{\beta}(P_{s})\cong P_{s}[a], then Σβ≅[a]\Sigma_{\beta}\cong[a].

2.5. The ℂ\mathbb{C}-action on 𝒯\mathcal{T} and t-exactness

The manifold Stab𝒞⁡(𝒯)\Stab_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathcal{T}) has a natural ℂ\mathbb{C}-action, which translates the slicing and scales the central charge: for z=a+π​i​b∈ℂz=a+\pi ib\in\mathbb{C} and τ=(𝒫,Z)\tau=(\mathcal{P},Z) define z⋅τ=(𝒫′,Z′)z\cdot\tau=(\mathcal{P}^{\prime},Z^{\prime}), where 𝒫′​(φ)=𝒫⁡(φ−b)\mathcal{P}^{\prime}(\varphi)=\mathcal{P}(\varphi-b) and Z′=ez​ZZ^{\prime}=e^{z}Z. Note this action commutes with all autoequivalences, i.e. gΣ​(z⋅τ)=z⋅gΣ​(τ)g_{\Sigma}(z\cdot\tau)=z\cdot g_{\Sigma}(\tau) for any autoequivalence Σ\Sigma. In particular, 𝖡\mathsf{B} acts on the quotient space Stab𝒞⁡(𝒯)/ℂ\Stab_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathcal{T})/\mathbb{C}.

Theorem 1.1 concerns elements of 𝖡\mathsf{B} that have a a fixed point in this space, i.e. β∈𝖡\beta\in\mathsf{B} such that β⋅τ=z⋅τ\beta\cdot\tau=z\cdot\tau for some τ∈Stab𝒞⁡(𝒯)\tau\in\Stab_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathcal{T}) and z∈ℂz\in\mathbb{C} . We explain how to interpret these fixed points from a homological point of view. Let us first recall a classical notion:

Definition 2.12.

Let Ψ:𝒯→𝒯\Psi:\mathcal{T}\to\mathcal{T} be an exact endofunctor and fix a heart ♡\heartsuit on 𝒯\mathcal{T}. The functor Ψ\Psi is said to be t-exact (with respect to ♡\heartsuit) if Ψ⁡(♡)⊆♡\Psi(\heartsuit)\subseteq\heartsuit; it is t-exact up to a shift m∈ℤm\in\mathbb{Z} if Ψ⁡(♡)⊆♡⁡[m]\Psi(\heartsuit)\subseteq\heartsuit[m].

Now suppose that Ψ⋅τ=z⋅τ\Psi\cdot\tau=z\cdot\tau for some τ∈Stab𝒞⁡(𝒯)\tau\in\Stab_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathcal{T}) and z=−m​π​i,m∈ℤz=-m\pi i,m\in\mathbb{Z}. Then Ψ(𝒫(0,1])=𝒫(m,m+1]\Psi(\mathcal{P}(0,1])=\mathcal{P}(m,m+1], and hence Ψ\Psi is t-exact up to shift mm with respect to the standard t-structure induced by 𝒫\mathcal{P}. From this perspective, a functor fixing a point in Stab𝒞⁡(𝒯)/ℂ\Stab_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathcal{T})/\mathbb{C} is a refinement of the notion of t-exactness.

Example 2.13.

Let Γ=A3\Gamma=A_{3}. We consider some examples of autoequivalences scaling a stability condition arising from the action of 𝖡\mathsf{B} on Stab⁡(𝒯)=Stab𝒞⁡(𝒯)\Stab(\mathcal{T})=\Stab_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathcal{T}).

  1. (1)

    The central element Θ\Theta acts by [2][2] on 𝒯\mathcal{T}, and hence acts by 2​π​i∈ℂ2\pi i\in\mathbb{C} on Stab𝒞⁡(𝒯)\Stab_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathcal{T}). Thus all points of Stab𝒞⁡(𝒯)/ℂ\Stab_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathcal{T})/\mathbb{C} are fixed by Θ\Theta.

  2. (2)

    Consider first the periodic element β≔σ1​σ2​σ3​σ1\beta\coloneqq\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2}\sigma_{3}\sigma_{1} in 𝖡\mathsf{B}. Define a stability condition τ∈Stab⁡(𝒯)\tau\in\Stab(\mathcal{T}) as in Figure 1 (left). In this stability condition the generating objects PiP_{i} are themselves stable, and we have drawn the central charge in the picture, putting the object PiP_{i} on the corresponding central charge vector. In this way the labelling in the figure defines both the slicing and the central charge. Note that the associated heart 𝒫(0,1]\mathcal{P}(0,1] of τ\tau is ♡std\heartsuit_{\std}, since Z⁡([Pi])∈ℍ∪ℝ<0Z([P_{i}])\in\mathbb{H}\cup\mathbb{R}_{<0} for i=1,2,3i=1,2,3. (The unlabelled vectors are the central charges of other stable objects.)

    A straightforward computation [19, Section 2.7] shows that β\beta acts on τ\tau by the complex number 2​π​i3\frac{2\pi i}{3} as depicted in Figure 1 (right). In other words, β⋅τ=2​π​i3⋅τ\beta\cdot\tau=\frac{2\pi i}{3}\cdot\tau and τ∈Stab⁡(𝒯)/ℂ\tau\in\Stab(\mathcal{T})/\mathbb{C} is a fixed point of β\beta.

  3. (3)

    Now consider the periodic element β′≔σ1​σ2​σ3\beta^{\prime}\coloneqq\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2}\sigma_{3} in 𝖡\mathsf{B}, and the stability condition given by Figure 2 (left). In this case, the heart 𝒫(0,1]\mathcal{P}(0,1] of τ\tau is given by σ3−1​(♡std)\sigma_{3}^{-1}(\heartsuit_{\std}) and the action of β′\beta^{\prime} rotates τ\tau by π2\frac{\pi}{2} as in Figure 2 (right), i.e. β′⋅τ′=π​i2⋅τ′\beta^{\prime}\cdot\tau^{\prime}=\frac{\pi i}{2}\cdot\tau^{\prime}.

In both examples the element in 𝖡\mathsf{B} rotates the stability condition by a scalar of the form x​π​ix\pi i, for some x∈ℚx\in\mathbb{Q}. This is a general phenomenon (Lemma 3.5). Note also that β3=β′4=Θ\beta^{3}={\beta^{\prime}}^{4}=\Theta is the full-twist, which acts on 𝒯\mathcal{T} by the triangulated shift [2][2] (Lemma 2.6). In other words, a power of these elements is t-exact up to shift. This is also a general phenomenon: those autoequivalences which scale stability conditions in Stab𝒞⁡(𝒯)\Stab_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathcal{T}) are roots of t-exact autoequivalences (cf. Section 3.2).

∎

3. Proof of the main theorem

This section is devoted to proving Theorem 1.1.

3.1. Forward implication using Springer theory

First we prove the forward direction of the theorem:

Proposition 3.1.

If β∈𝖡\beta\in\mathsf{B} is periodic then there is a point in Stab𝒞⁡(𝒯)/ℂ\Stab_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathcal{T})/\mathbb{C} that it is fixed by β\beta.

Bessis’ Springer theory for braid groups allows us to make an immediate simplification:

Lemma 3.2.

If for every regular integer dd there exists a dd-th root of Θ\Theta that fixes a point in Stab𝒞⁡(𝒯)/ℂ\Stab_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathcal{T})/\mathbb{C}, then Proposition 3.1 follows.

Proof.

Note that if β\beta has a fixed point in Stab𝒞⁡(𝒯)/ℂ\Stab_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathcal{T})/\mathbb{C} then so does any power of β\beta. Therefore it suffices prove Proposition 3.1 for primitive periodic elements (recall β\beta is primitive if β=γk\beta=\gamma^{k} implies k=±1k=\pm 1 for all γ∈𝖡\gamma\in\mathsf{B}). By [18, Theorem 3.14] any primitive periodic element is a root of Θ\Theta.

So now we’ve reduced the problem to finding a fixed point for dd-th roots of Θ\Theta, where dd is any positive integer. By part (i) of Theorem 2.4, dd is regular for 𝖶\mathsf{W}. Now if τ∈Stab𝒞⁡(𝒯)/ℂ\tau\in\Stab_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathcal{T})/\mathbb{C} is a fixed point for β\beta, then γ⋅τ\gamma\cdot\tau is a fixed point for γ​β​γ−1\gamma\beta\gamma^{-1}. Moreover, by part (ii) of Theorem 2.4, there is a single conjugacy class of dd-th roots of Θ\Theta in 𝖡\mathsf{B}. Hence, it suffices to find, for every regular integer dd, a fixed point for some dd-th root of Θ\Theta. ∎

Now fix a regular integer dd. By Lemma 3.2, to prove Proposition 3.1 it suffices to find a dd-th root of Θ\Theta which fixes some stability condition in Stab𝒞⁡(𝒯)/ℂ\Stab_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathcal{T})/\mathbb{C}. Let ζd=e2​π​id\zeta_{d}=e^{\frac{2\pi i}{d}}. By classical Springer theory, there exists w∈𝖶,Z∈ℋw\in\mathsf{W},Z\in\mathcal{H} such that w⋅Z=ζd​Zw\cdot Z=\zeta_{d}Z. The image Z¯∈ℋ/𝖶\overline{Z}\in\mathcal{H}/\mathsf{W} of the eigenvector ZZ provides the central charge for our sought-after stability condition. To lift it to a stability condition, we use that π:Stab𝒞⁡(𝒯)→ℋ/𝖶\pi:\Stab_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathcal{T})\to\mathcal{H}/\mathsf{W} is a (universal) cover (see Theorem 2.7(1)). We’ll now show that τ0\tau_{0} is fixed point for a dd-th root of Θ\Theta.

By Theorem 2.7(2), there exists β∈𝖡\beta\in\mathsf{B} such that fλ=gβf_{\lambda}=g_{\beta}. By Lemma 2.10 we have that fϑ=gΘ.f_{\vartheta}=g_{\Theta}. Hence, we have that

So β\beta is a dd-th root of Θ\Theta, and we’ll now show it fixes τ0∈Stab𝒞⁡(𝒯)/ℂ\tau_{0}\in\Stab_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathcal{T})/\mathbb{C}. First, lift λ\lambda to a path λ~\widetilde{\lambda} in Stab𝒞⁡(𝒯)\Stab_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathcal{T}) beginning at τ0\tau_{0}, and let τ1\tau_{1} be its endpoint. By construction, τ1=λ⋅τ0=β⋅τ0\tau_{1}=\lambda\cdot\tau_{0}=\beta\cdot\tau_{0}. Hence, τ1=z⋅τ0\tau_{1}=z\cdot\tau_{0} for some z∈ℝz\in\mathbb{R} (in fact, z=1dz=\frac{1}{d} but we don’t need that here). We’ve now shown that β⋅τ0=z⋅τ0\beta\cdot\tau_{0}=z\cdot\tau_{0}. Remark 3.3.

Observe that our proof of Proposition 3.1 did not use any intrinsic properties of the space Stab𝒞⁡(𝒯)\Stab_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathcal{T}), and indeed this argument would work for any universal cover of ℋ/𝖶\mathcal{H}/\mathsf{W}. More precisely, if π:Y→ℋ/𝖶\pi:Y\to\mathcal{H}/\mathsf{W} is any universal cover, then YY is naturally endowed with a ℂ\mathbb{C}-action since ℂ×\mathbb{C}^{\times} acts on ℋ/𝖶\mathcal{H}/\mathsf{W}. Now choose any point Z¯∈ℋ/𝖶\overline{Z}\in\mathcal{H}/\mathsf{W} and any isomorphism 𝖡→π1​(ℋ/𝖶,Z¯)\mathsf{B}\to\pi_{1}(\mathcal{H}/\mathsf{W},\overline{Z}), thereby endowing YY with a 𝖡\mathsf{B}-action (which commutes with the ℂ\mathbb{C}-action). Then the same proof as above gives: if β\beta is periodic then β\beta has a fixed point in Y/ℂY/\mathbb{C}. On the other hand, our argument for the other direction of Theorem 1.1 uses the modular description of the universal cover as a space of stability conditions (cf. Remark 3.7).

To complete the proof of Theorem 1.1 we prove:

If β∈𝖡\beta\in\mathsf{B} has a fixed point in τ∈Stab𝒞⁡(𝒯)/ℂ\tau\in\Stab_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathcal{T})/\mathbb{C}, i.e. β⋅τ=z⋅τ\beta\cdot\tau=z\cdot\tau for some z∈ℂz\in\mathbb{C}, then β\beta is periodic.

Remark 3.7.

Lemma 3.6 is the only part of our argument where the stability space as a moduli space of categorical structures is used in an essential way. In particular, both the categorical rigidity Lemma 2.11 and faithfulness of the categorical action (Theorem 2.7(2)) are used in the above argument.

4. Future work

Motivation for this work comes from an ongoing program to develop a dynamical theory for autoequivalence groups of triangulated categories. A model theorem from topology is the Nielsen–Thurston classification [24], which gives a dynamical classification of elements in the mapping class group of a (compact orientable) surface. In this classification, two dynamical classes – periodic and pseudo-Anosov – form the basic building blocks used to understand the dynamics of an arbitrary mapping class. Moreover, the action of the mapping class group on the Teichmüller space of the surface plays an important role in this theory: periodic maps have a fixed point in Teichmüller space whereas pseudo-Anosov maps have a pair of fixed points in its Thurston boundary.

The Nielson-Thurston classification does not directly give rise to a dynamical classification of elements in finite type Artin–Tits groups. Indeed, finite type Artin–Tits groups typically do not arise as (subgroups of) surface mapping class groups [26]. However, Theorem 1.1 is a step towards an analogous categorical Nielsen–Thurston classification, which should apply not just to finite type Artin–Tits groups but also to a larger family of triangulated autoequivalence groups, such as the autoequivalence group of the derived category of a K3 surface.

In this sense, Theorem 1.1 is part of the larger program to understand autoequivalence groups of triangulated categories with metrics. In this program, the triangulated category itself is thought of as something akin to the topological Fukaya category of a surface, and, in the presence of a triangulated metric such as a stability condition, an autoequivalence is studied via the discrete dynamical system it defines [11]. Next steps in this program should involve developing the dynamical theory of elements in 𝖡\mathsf{B} which give rise to pseudo-Anosov autoequivalences [14] and studying the action of these autoequivalences on the compactifications of [1].
